claim: At the end of January 1857 Mark Thornhill, magistrate at Mathura (Muttra), found four small cakes of coarse flour on his office table; a man had given one cake to a village watchman (chowkidar) with orders to bake four like it and give them to the watchmen of the adjacent villages, who were to do the same.

sources.title: Mark Thornhill, The Personal Adventures and Experiences of a Magistrate during the Rise, Progress and Suppression of the Indian Mutiny (London, 1884), ch. I, pp. 2-3 (Internet Archive full text)
sources.quote: It was at the end of January 1857 ... I found four little cakes laid on the table, dirty little cakes of the coarsest flour ... A man had come to a village, and given a cake to the watchman, with injunctions to bake four like it, to distribute them to the watchmen of the adjacent villages, and to desire them to do the same.

sources.title: Mike Dash, 'The chupatty movement' (A Blast From The Past, 2010; author of the Smithsonian article 'Pass it on'), citing Thornhill, Kaye, Hibbert, Ireland and Kim A. Wagner, The Great Fear of 1857 (2010)
sources.quote: four 'dirty little cakes of the coarsest flour, about the size and thickness of a biscuit'

sources.title: Wikipedia, 'Mark Thornhill'

qualification: say मथुरा के मजिस्ट्रेट; 'four' is Thornhill's number (other accounts give other numbers)
notes: Dash dates it 'early February'; Thornhill's own text says end of January 1857. Narration gives no month for this scene.

claim: The cakes were being distributed the same way over all 'Upper India' (north India) in early 1857; popular accounts say from the Narmada to the Nepal border.

claim: Many contemporaries read the chapatis as a signal or warning of a coming outbreak ('a kind of fiery cross, to call them to action'; 'a forerunner of some universal popular outbreak'); Collector Ford of Gurgaon reported 'a signal' whose purport had not transpired.

qualification: a theory held by some officials, framed 'कुछ अफ़सरों को लगा'
